findings.statement: fsync is not the dominant cost of publishing a checkpoint
findings.detail: 915 ops/s with fsync against 26019 without (28.4x). Every read-your-writes operation costs a checkpoint and a checkpoint syncs twice, so this is what durability costs on the workload the engine is worst at (nosync vs sync: greater 28.437x (p=0.0122, rel_iqr 2.2%/6.9%))

findings.statement: removing fsync is worth less than removing the block table decode was
findings.detail: fsync is worth 28.4x here. Mapping the block table removed 34% of all instructions -- 4.75x fewer in total -- and moved throughput by nothing. An instruction profile answers where the CPU goes, not why a workload is slow, and those differ whenever the answer is a syscall

notes: read-your-writes shape: half the operations write, and a read after a write costs a checkpoint plus a reader reopen. Both arms interleaved; the only difference is Options::sync_on_checkpoint
